extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political philosophy (readers of Plato)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical exposition (Plato's Republic, Book VIII) that categorizes five forms of government (aristocracy, timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny) and the corresponding character-types, explaining their origins, defects, transitions, and implications for happiness and civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-kings as rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the true philosopher kings are born in a State, despising the honours of this present world, esteeming above all things right and the honour that springs from right, and regarding justice as the greatest and most necessary of all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers should make philosophy their chief pursuit, rule as a matter of duty (not for honours), set the pattern of the State by the vision of the absolute good, train successors, and after distinguished public service retire (at or after fifty) to be honoured. Their rule is presented as the ideal basis for a just State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of women in guardian roles
rubrics_metrics.description: What has been said applies to men and to women as far as their natures can go; women are to share in all things like the men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women, to the extent of their capacity, should receive the same training and share in civic and guardian responsibilities—this is part of the constitution of the perfect State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal families and property among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: In the perfect State wives and children are to be in common; all education and the pursuits of war and peace are also to be common; rulers will live in houses common to all and contain nothing private; no one was to have any of the ordinary possessions of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians are to be maintained (not paid privately), live communally, eat common meals, and hold no private property in order to prevent personal interests from corrupting public duty and to preserve unity and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended staged education and service for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Children are to be taken and trained from about ten years old; periods of bodily exercise and other stages of training (e.g., five years, then fifteen years) lead to experience and then to philosophical study, culminating in rule around fifty years of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guardian class undergoes long, staged education—physical training, military/political experience, and finally philosophy—so that only those fully formed in virtue and knowledge rule; age and tested life-experience are criteria for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of marriages and births to preserve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be laws controlling the timing and partners of unions among guardians; ignorance of the 'law of births' and untimely unions produce unworthy offspring and weaken the ruling class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breeding and marriage should be regulated (the text appeals to numerical/harmonic patterns) to maintain the 'metal' quality of the citizenry (gold, silver, brass, iron) and avoid mixing that brings inequality, hatred, and war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of music and gymnastics in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy tempered with music is the saviour of virtue; neglecting music and favouring gymnastics alone leads to a decline in cultivation and a shift toward spirited/martial characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural education (music, arts) must temper physical education; overvaluing gymnastics and neglecting music/philosophy produces timocratic characters prone to ambition and contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as the ideal and the benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: The true form (aristocracy governed by the best/philosophers) is the ideal; other forms are deviations (timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny) and should be compared to it to judge their justice and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the aristocratic/philosophical State as the standard when assessing other regimes; the inquiry aims to determine which constitution yields the happiest life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocracy arises from partial loss of philosophical guardianship
rubrics_metrics.description: Timocracy (government of honour) results when guardians neglect philosophy and music and place more value on military qualities and honour; it is characterised by contention and ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timocratic States emphasise martial training and honour, fear admitting philosophers, engage in continual warfare, honour gymnastic over music, and may secretly covet money despite ostensible disdain for riches; this mixture of spirited elements leads to specific social pathologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property qualification as basis of oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy is a government resting on a valuation of property, in which the rich have power and the poor are deprived of it; laws fix a sum of money as the qualification for citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using wealth as the criterion for political participation excludes capable but poor citizens, produces a divided State (rich vs poor), and leads to social and military weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evils/defects of oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects include the inevitable division into two States (rich and poor), incapacity to carry on war (either arming the multitude or being too few to fight), reluctance to tax, extremes of wealth and poverty, and the proliferation of paupers and criminal 'drones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchic institutions foster social instability, crime, and loss of civic unity; the valuation of wealth undermines virtue and effective governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the oligarchical (avaricious) man
rubrics_metrics.description: The oligarchical man is penurious and laborious, values wealth above cultivation, restricts desires to necessities, coerces bad passions by fear of loss rather than reason, and may become dishonest when handling others' property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological profile mirrors the State: outwardly respectable but internally divided; preserved by fear of loss rather than genuine virtue; vulnerable to corruption when opportunity allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy arising from oligarchic abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy comes into being when the poor revolt against oligarchy, give equal freedom and power (magistrates often chosen by lot), and the city becomes full of freedom, variety, and frankness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracy is celebrated for liberty and pluralism (an 'embroidered robe' of many types), but its freedoms can lead to disregard for cultivated principles and may be only momentarily delightful; it permits a wide assortment of constitutions and lifestyles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom vs. discipline trade-off in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracy there is maximal individual freedom—one may order one's life as one pleases—which produces variety of human natures and a forgiving spirit, but also a decline in the observance of earlier 'fine principles' of education and civic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive freedom can erode the disciplined practices (education in beauty, music, and virtue) that undergird the best citizens; democracy's strengths (liberty, variety) are also sources of potential civic decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics of constitutional change (sequence and causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments vary as the dispositions of men vary; constitutions change through divisions of governing power and social causes—sequence given: aristocracy -> timocracy -> oligarchy -> democracy -> tyranny—driven by causes like mis-breeding, accumulation of wealth, neglect of philosophy, and internal faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand regime transitions as arising from moral/educational and economic shifts within the citizenry; diagnosing causes (e.g., mixing of metals/metaphors, private wealth accumulation) explains how each form deteriorates into the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of happiness to judge regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry aims to compare whether the best (just) man and the best State are also the happiest, and whether the worst (unjust) are the most miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of constitutions ultimately hinge on whether they produce happiness for their citizens; the moral question of whether justice yields true happiness is central to judging political forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private wealth as corrosive of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of gold in private treasuries ruins timocracy; as men think more of making a fortune they think less of virtue, and when riches and virtue are placed together the one rises as the other falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing private wealth to become an object of honour displaces virtuous aims, corrupts public values, and sets the State on the path toward oligarchy and social decay.
